questionText:
Consider the following sets:

S1. Set of all recursively enumerable languages over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$
S2. Set of all syntactically valid C programs
S3. Set of all languages over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$
S4. Set of all non-regular languages over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$

Which of the above sets are uncountable?
explanation:
Analysis of each set:

S1: Set of all recursively enumerable languages over $\{0,1\}$
Every recursively enumerable language is accepted by a Turing machine. Since the set of all Turing machines is countably infinite, the set of recursively enumerable languages is countable.

S2: Set of all syntactically valid C programs
Every valid C program is a string of finite length over a finite alphabet (ASCII). The set of all finite length strings over a finite alphabet is countably infinite, so the set of syntactically valid C programs is countable.

S3: Set of all languages over $\{0,1\}$
The set of all strings $\{0,1\}^*$ is countably infinite. A language over $\{0,1\}$ is defined as any subset of $\{0,1\}^*$. The set of all languages is the power set $\mathcal{P}(\{0,1\}^*)$, which is uncountable (cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$).

S4: Set of all non-regular languages over $\{0,1\}$
The set of all regular languages is countable because each regular language can be uniquely represented by a deterministic finite automaton (DFA). Since the total set of languages is uncountable and the set of regular languages is countable, the remaining set of non-regular languages must be uncountable.

Therefore, sets S3 and S4 are uncountable, which corresponds to option (B).
